title: Symphony No. 9 in D minor
hook: Bruckner’s last symphony, said to be dedicated “to the beloved God”, ends with a slow farewell; he died before finishing the finale.

painting.title: The Angelus
painting.pairingNote: Two farm workers stop to pray at the evening bell: the plain country faith of Bruckner, a village schoolmaster’s son, who dedicated this last symphony “to the beloved God”.

facts: Bruckner began the symphony in August 1887 and worked on it, with long interruptions for revising his earlier symphonies, until his death in Vienna on 11 October 1896, aged 72. The first three movements were finished by November 1894; the finale was left as a mass of sketches.
According to his early biographers, he said he was dedicating his last work “to the beloved God”, and hoped God would give him time to complete it.

It is usually played, as here, in three movements: a vast first movement, a fierce [[scherzo|scherzo]], and a slow Adagio that ends in peace. Bruckner called the Adagio’s chorale his “farewell to life”.
Like Beethoven’s Ninth, it is in D minor and puts the scherzo second. The orchestra has eight horns, four of which switch to [[wagner-tuba|Wagner tuba]]s in the Adagio.
The first performance, in Vienna in 1903 under Ferdinand Löwe, used Löwe’s heavily altered version. Bruckner’s own score was not heard until 1932, in Munich.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dark, cathedral-sized struggle (I), a demonic dance with a ghostly trio (II), a long farewell that finds peace (III).

movements.heading: Feierlich, misterioso
movements.summary: “Solemn, mysterious.” Out of a trembling D, the horns intone a dark motif, and the music grows slowly to a huge theme played by the whole orchestra in octaves. Then come two more groups of themes, one yearning and one mysterious. The rest of the movement develops and restates them together, and the end is not a victory but a blazing, dissonant clash.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: a [[tremolo|tremolo]] on D in the strings, with a slow, dark horn motif.

mainIdeas.name: The octave theme
mainIdeas.description: a huge, falling theme for the whole orchestra in [[unison|unison]], with a long-held note and a plunge of an octave.

mainIdeas.name: The second group
mainIdeas.description: a broad, yearning melody in the violins, slower.

mainIdeas.name: The third group
mainIdeas.description: quiet woodwind phrases over shimmering strings, then a mysterious, rocking theme in unison.

stops.hear: The strings tremble very softly on one note; the horns intone a slow, dark motif
stops.happening: The first group of themes begins, in D minor

stops.hear: The horns suddenly blaze out a bright fanfare in a new key
A long crescendo, then the whole orchestra plays one huge theme in octaves
stops.happening: The octave theme, at full power. It falls away into silence

stops.hear: Slower and quiet: the violins sing a broad, yearning melody
stops.happening: The second group, in A major

stops.hear: Soft woodwind phrases over shimmering strings, then a strange, rocking theme in unison
Soft horn calls under a haze; then the dark horn motif of the opening returns
stops.happening: The [[development|development]], which also restates the themes

stops.hear: A long climb to a thunderous climax for the full orchestra
stops.happening: The octave theme returns at its most violent

stops.hear: The yearning violin melody again
The quiet woodwinds and the rocking theme again
A slow, enormous build-up over a held bass

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The opening fanfare in the trumpets, grinding against the rest of the orchestra; bare, loud D chords

notice: Listen to the silences. Bruckner often stops the whole orchestra dead, then starts again in a new colour, like an organist changing stops.
In the last bars the music does not resolve into warmth: it ends on bare fifths with a clashing note on top.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Bernard Haitink was 83 when he conducted the symphony with the London Symphony Orchestra at two concerts in the Barbican in February 2013. He uses Leopold Nowak’s edition of Bruckner’s own score.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Bewegt, lebhaft – Trio: Schnell
movements.summary: A menacing, stamping [[scherzo|scherzo]]. It starts with a bar of silence, then strange, sour woodwind chords over plucked strings, before the whole orchestra hammers out a brutal rhythm. In the middle, the [[trio|trio]] is fast, light and eerie, in the distant key of F-sharp major. Then the scherzo returns.

mainIdeas.name: The opening chord
mainIdeas.description: a sour, unresolved woodwind chord, repeated, over [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] strings.

mainIdeas.name: The hammering
mainIdeas.description: the full orchestra pounding the same chord in a heavy, stamping rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: quick, flickering string figures, light and ghostly, with a slower, singing middle.

stops.hear: A moment of silence, then soft, sour woodwind chords over plucked strings
The whole orchestra hammers out the chord in a heavy, stamping rhythm
Lighter: the oboe leads a short, dance-like tune
Fast, flickering strings in a new, bright key
Slower, a singing string melody
stops.happening: The calm middle of the trio

stops.hear: The soft, sour chords and plucked strings return
stops.happening: The scherzo again, repeated as before

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The stamping rhythm, ending with a crash
stops.happening: A brutal end in D minor

notice: Listen to the very first chord. It belongs to no single key, and Bruckner repeats it again and again without explaining it. Many listeners hear this scherzo as the most modern music Bruckner wrote.

movements.heading: Adagio: Langsam, feierlich
movements.summary: “Slow, solemn.” The violins open alone with an anguished upward leap. The movement unfolds in two great paragraphs, the first searching and painful, the second consoling, and they return and grow. At the height of the last climax the music breaks on a shattering discord. After a silence, the movement ends in calm.

mainIdeas.name: The opening theme
mainIdeas.description: violins alone, leaping upward and then sinking through strange harmonies.

mainIdeas.name: The trumpet fanfare
mainIdeas.description: a call repeated again and again over the whole orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: The “farewell to life”
mainIdeas.description: a slow, sinking [[chorale|chorale]] for horns and Wagner tubas.

mainIdeas.name: The consoling theme
mainIdeas.description: a broad, warm melody in the strings.

stops.hear: The violins alone leap upward, then sink; the dark Wagner tubas join
stops.happening: The opening theme, far from any clear key

stops.hear: The music builds, and the trumpets ring out a repeated fanfare over the whole orchestra
Horns and Wagner tubas in a slow, descending chorale
The strings sing a broad, warm, consoling melody
After a silence, the opening theme returns, now with a new flute line around it
stops.happening: The first paragraph returns and is developed

stops.hear: The consoling melody returns, with swirling violin figures over plucked basses, and begins a long climb
A deafening, dissonant chord for the whole orchestra, then silence
stops.happening: The catastrophe at the top of the climax

stops.label: Last 3 minutes
stops.hear: Quiet, slow music; the Wagner tubas and horns recall earlier symphonies; a soft, long E major chord

notice: Listen to the end. The Wagner tubas play a phrase from the Adagio of Bruckner’s Eighth Symphony, and the horns recall the opening of his Seventh: a last look back.

threads.title: A symphony without an end
threads.body: Bruckner meant to write a finale, but died working on it. Played in three movements, the symphony ends with the slow Adagio, and many hear that as fitting.

threads.title: Faith and farewell
threads.body: The dedication “to the beloved God”, the chorale Bruckner called his “farewell to life”, the quiet end: this is the most personal of his symphonies.

threads.title: Bold harmony
threads.body: The sour chord that opens the scherzo, the discord at the Adagio’s climax: Bruckner, the conservative organist, wrote some of the most daring sounds of the 1890s.
